source.title: Ouroboros: Dynamic Weight Generation for Recursive Transformers via Input-Conditioned LoRA Modulation

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. The front matter dates the arXiv version to 2026, while a footer says NeurIPS 2023; the supplied venue field is blank.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports language-model loss after adapting pretrained Qwen models. It does not test random-initialization training error on classification benchmarks or any listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The paper's training-loss results concern pretrained language models and next-token prediction, not training classification error on CIFAR or the listed version-specific settings. They are recorded as findings about the related training outcome under fits_no_version. The paper also cites prior recurrence work; those cited results are not extracted as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates its own adaptation method on pretrained Qwen transformers using language-model loss. It neither tests nor relies on any listed claim version. Its recurrence, gating, initialization and learning-rate experiments do not measure the specific effects named in V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors report lower training-distribution loss, an advantage over static per-step LoRA, and a benefit from gating in a separate recursive-refinement experiment, but no held-out improvement over the truncated baseline. Their attribution of generalization failure to frozen coda layers, and prediction that adapting those layers would resolve it, remain hypotheses rather than demonstrated results.
record.recipe_differences: The study adapts pretrained Qwen language models using a Controller and recursive LoRA modulation; it does not use the claim's random-initialization classification-training recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported training-distribution loss is similar across tested Controller depths and ranks; the study says learning rate matters slightly. Gated versus ungated recurrence changes the loss outcome. Held-out evaluation differs from training-distribution results.

fits_no_version.finding: Controller configurations achieve training-distribution language-model losses of 5.073–5.082 versus 8.975 for the 17-layer baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Controller-modulated adaptation reduces training-distribution loss in the tested pretrained Qwen2.5-3B architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: The Controller has lower loss than static per-step LoRA in each reported paired comparison; the depth-1 difference is 1.437 points.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Input-conditioned Controller modulation outperforms static per-step diagonal modulation on training-distribution loss in the tested adaptation recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: In the separate Qwen2.5-0.5B experiment, ungated recursive refinement raises loss by 0.20, while gated refinement lowers loss from 9.42 to 5.93.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gated recurrence improves the loss outcome of the tested pretrained-transformer recursive-refinement setup.

fits_no_version.finding: On 12 held-out passages, the adapted model has average loss 5.961 versus 5.690 for the truncated baseline, beating it on 3 passages.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The reported training-distribution improvement does not transfer to lower average loss on the tested held-out passages.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2023 is stated in a footer; supplied venue field is blank and the paper text also dates the arXiv version to 2026.
record.problems: The training results use pretrained models and language-model loss, so they do not establish classification-error outcomes in the claim. Held-out evaluation uses only 12 passages. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the extracted results.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-version rows were applicable. Results for mitigation variants (dropout, mixed training data, constrained LoRA scaling) are summarized only in text without separate values for each variant, apart from the best constrained variant's held-out gap change; these do not measure any listed version.

untested.parts: All parts: random-initialization convolutional-network training, CIFAR classification error, label corruption, model size, early stopping and regularization.
All parts: two-layer ReLU teacher-student optimization, spurious local minima and student overparameterization.
All parts: training-error degradation in plain convolutional networks, identity-shortcut comparisons and the stated initialization and normalization exceptions.
All parts: comparative effects of activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, learning speed and trainable depth in plain networks.
All parts: learning rates relative to initial stability thresholds, transient loss increases, curvature changes, edge-of-stability dynamics and divergence.
All parts: batch normalization versus its absence, accuracy gain speed, learning-rate tolerance and Fixup comparisons. Per-step RMSNorm is not a batch-normalization ablation.

record.verdict_notes: All rows remain linked to none. Their states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V6, even where the separate method-performance outcome is clear. Method comparisons belong under fits_no_version rather than serving as evidence for these versions. No additional result bearing on a listed version was found in the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, random or corrupted labels, random initialization, model size, and early stopping.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious local minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus residual convolutional networks, classification training error by depth, and the stated special-initialization and normalization conditions.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, and trainable depth in plain networks.
Learning rates relative to stability or sharpness thresholds, loss curvature, and divergence.
Batch normalization's effect on accuracy speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.
